artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Two forms, which seem to be designed out of musical notes on scores, are drawn in red and blue. The heads and lines of each four notes are connected to form a single entity; one of the red heads is filled in green. Above these are two phrases written in the same colors as the images below. “For Ayako” is written in blue, and “For Rieko” is written in red. This work may have been created for the two daughters of Shuya Abe, the Japanese technician, who had formed a close relationship with Nam June Paik.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: “Thank you very much for everything, Gyeonggi Governor Lim. It will definitely be a great success. Nam June Paik, February 1st, 2002, MiAMi.” is written in a combination of Chinese, Korean, and English characters. The drawing seems to hold Nam June Paik’s wish for a successful opening of the Nam June Paik museum. Drawn in the background is a human face with earphones that seem to enjoy listening to something through a satellite. Above the word “SATELLite” in the upper-left corner, Paik added a form of a planet, which suggests the often-employed concept of space communication.

artworks.description: Whenever artistic ideas came to mind, Nam June Paik whimsically scribbled them out, unhesitatingly on whatever was available at the moment, on the margins of book pages or restaurant’s napkins. Yet he would also build ideas cumulatively in a notebook. This drawing book was donated by Shuya Abe, Paik’s technical collaborator. In this sketchbook, Paik drew a simplified form of the television with an antenna on each page, and inside the TV, four characters of Shuya Abe’s name was written, respectively. Also, the Chinese character ‘色’ was written repeatedly in various colors, on several pages.…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: TV color bars that Nam June Paik frequently used in his videos can also be found in his paintings. In Untitled, eight color bars of white, yellow, light blue, green, pink, red, dark blue, and black are repeated in four rows, moving one column to the left in each row. Two white canvases are attached to the canvas in oblique directions. The left canvas displays the sun, a TV set, and human faces overlapped with black lines in the form of large Vs, along with the word “LION” written above. On the right, a round face is repeated numerously like a pattern.

artworks.title: Hommage à Jean-Pierre Wilhelm, Dusseldorf
artworks.description: “걷는다, 뛴다, 행인들을 바라본다, 생각에 잠긴다, 웃는다.” Nam June Paik은 Manfred Leve에게 이런 무의미해 보이는 행동을 찍어 달라고 청했다. Venue는 갤러리 22가 location했던 곳으로, Nam June Paik이 〈존 케이지에 대한 경의: 테이프와 피아노를 위한 음악〉(1958)을 처음 발표할 수 있었던 곳이다. 당시 25살 이었던 Nam June Paik은 다름슈타트 국제 현대음악 하기강좌에서 자신의 첫 곡을 발표하기 위해 노심초사하고 있었다. 그러나 그 일은 잘 성사되지 않았고 낙심한 Nam June Paik에게 손을 내민 사람은 갤러리 22를 운영하던 장피에르 빌헬름이었다. 이후 빌헬름은 Nam June Paik을 비롯한 플럭서스의 든든한 후원자가 되었다. 빌헬름이 세상을 떠난 지 10년 후, Nam June Paik은 가장 평범한 일상의 행동을 통해 빌헬름을 추모했다. 삶의 미디어와 예술의 미디어가 하나가 되는 순간, Nam June Paik 스스로가 가장 의미 있는 인터미디어가 되었다.

artworks.title: UNTITLED
artworks.description: Heavy raindrops, painted in white, fall on a straw-thatched gazebo. Above the rain streaks are green dots running parallel with the white dots; the dots resemble the alphabet “V” at a closer look, which Nam June Paik often used to portray an old television’s antenna. Behind the rain are books, and behind the falling Vs is a furrow-like lattice structure. At the bottom of the painting is a Chinese four-character idiom, 晴耕雨讀, meaning “working in the field in fine weather and reading at home in wet weather.” Paik had stressed the importance of studying from the 1960s, which he had strived to…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Nam June Paik never gave up his will to create, think radically, and study despite his collapse from a stroke in 1996. Paik primarily worked on painting in the 2000s, as his physical constraints grew worse, yet the artist’s insight in life and artistic concept were portrayed in his typical immediate and humorous way. This work portrays the Avalokiteshvara with a thousand arms, one of his often-depicted motifs, in simplified lines. Written below are the Buddha’s Chinese name and part of a Buddhist prayer.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: This work is composed of diverse squares and rectangles; two smaller rectangles seem to represent television sets, while the other two appear to portray houses. A TV set is located inside the house on the right, whereas the TV set on the left is located outside, surrounded by dotted lines. Recalling Paik’s rendition of communication connected by a broadcast network by employing dotted lines, this design-like drawing may embody the television not as a passive and enclosed media but as a two-way media open to the world.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: This work reads, “Piano Rhapsody For Steve Vitiello” with a couple of misspellings. The lower part looks like a musical score of horizontal lines and simplified notes, with the numbers 33, 45, 78 added, which may refer to the playing speed of LPs. Video and sound artist Stephen Vitiello was greatly influenced by Nam June Paik when they first met in 1991. Vitiello filmed Paik’s performance Piano Concert in SeOUL-NYmAx: A Celebration of Arts without Borders in 1994 and 1997, and also collaborated with Paik for his Tiger Lives in 1999 and Modulation in Sync in 2000.

artworks.title: Sky Kiss, Ars Electronica, Linz
artworks.description: Charlotte Moorman performed Sky Kiss in collaboration with Jim McWilliams from 1968. Graphic designer and composer McWilliams conceived a scene of Moorman with the cello’s endpin drifting aloft from the ground meeting an immaterial lover, out of his desire to represent the erotic subject of kissing, often depicted in art history, in an unconventional form. Moorman was to float with a helium-filled balloon and play the cello in mid-air. The first attempt was made in Philadelphia in March 1968, yet the balloon did not rise. In the 6th Annual Avant-Garde Festival of New York that took place…

artworks.title: Jean-Pierre Wilhelm’s Retire Happening, Joseph Beuys’ house, Dusseldorf
artworks.description: This is a photograph of the 1967 happening of Jean-Pierre Wilhelm’s retirement address made to the art world at Joseph Beuys’ house in Dusseldorf. In his writing, Beuys Vox (1986), Nam June Paik referred to the event as one of the most important incidents of the year. “Already in his fifties and aware of his impending death, Wilhelm along with Manfred Leve came to Beuys’ apartment where Charlotte and I stayed. While having a chat, he took a piece of paper out of his pocket and recited a declaration of goodbye to his official art life. The moment was photographed by Dr. Leve. After Wilhelm…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: In this work, Nam June Paik wrote a list of names or pseudonyms of Korean literary giants such as Lee Eun-sang, Lyuh Woon-hyung, Park Jong-hwa, Lee Tae-jun, Yi Kwang-su, Jeong Ji-yong, and Kim Sowol. At the center of the picture plane are fourteen consonants of Hangul, the Korean alphabet, and in between the alphabets are four Chinese characters in light blue, meaning the Buddhist Elysium; below are the basic characters of Hangul in orange. The rest comprises Chinese four-character idioms. 女慕貞烈 男效才良: Women should follow the right-hearted and the strong-willed, and men should follow the…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: In this work, Nam June Paik notated part of the Korean song I shall live at Geumgang, composed by Hong Nan-pa. The word ‘prelude’ added on the lower-left corner seems to indicate that the notated part is the first two bars of the song. The song’s lyrics are traditional Korean three-stanza poems written by the poet Lee Eun-sang, Lee wrote the poem, expressing his wish to live in the picturesque scenery, away from the world, when he went to Mt. Geumgang in 1930,. From his earlier days, Paik paid much attention to the Korean sentiment embodied in traditional literature, and composed music…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: This work includes flowers, the sun, a heart, and a comical female nude. As written on the lower-left corner, Nam June Paik depicts the Garden of Eden in the Book of Genesis. Far from sophistication, the seemingly haphazard scribbling reflects the artist’s frustration caused by the aftermath of his illness on the one hand; the energy that primary colors and reckless lines deliver, however, also emanates Paik’s ceaseless aspirations for art-making.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: From the Thousand Character Classic, a Chinese poem arranged into 250 lines of four characters apiece, Nam June Paik wrote nine fourcharacter idioms in different colors. 律呂調陽: Six bright sounds and six dark sounds are brought to balance yin and yang. 日月盁昃 辰宿列張: The sun and the moon naturally wax and wane, and a constellation of stars is spread out on the sky. 寒來暑往 秋收冬藏: When the cold comes, the heat is gone; you harvest a crop in autumn, and store up on it in winter. 雲騰致雨 露結爲霜: Clouds rise up to become rain, and dewdrops get tangles to become frost. 始制文字 乃服衣裳: Letters were created at last…

artworks.title: Zen for Walking, 12th Annual Avant-Garde Festival of New York, Floyd Bennett Field, New York
artworks.medium: black & white photograph on baryta paper
artworks.description: In 1961, Nam June Paik walked around the streets of Cologne, Germany, dragging a violin behind him. The performance is called Zen for Walking and alternately Violin with String (Dragging Violin in the Street). Paik repeated the performance many times up to 1975, when Peter Moore photographed him dragging a violin around Brooklyn’s Floyd Bennett Field Park as part of the 12th Annual New York Avant-Garde Festival. Paik has said of these performances that dragging an instrument on the streets made them produce beautiful sounds.

artworks.title: Fluxus Sonata No. 4, Anthology Film Archives, New York
artworks.medium: black & white photograph on baryta paper
artworks.description: During the construction of the new Anthology Film Archives site on 80 Wooster Street, New York, in 1973, Nam June Paik performed a series of the Fluxus Sonata in the venue, beginning with Fluxus Sonata No. 1. The photograph shows a performance of Fluxus Sonata No. 4 in 1975. In front of several turntables, Paik put an LP on one of them and listened carefully with his arms crossed; and then he moved to another turntable to activate another LP. With the two vinyl records rotating simultaneously, he oscillated between the phonographs, interrupting and spinning them with his hands. Physically…

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: In this drawing of a female body, facial features are left out; instead, the middle part formed by the chest, navel, and genitals appear to be the eyes, nose, and mouth. Nam June Paik often drew female nudes with humor, to render the furtive subject in a vivacious way. Over the waves of the sea where a boat is afloat at the bottom of the drawing reads “Hamptons.” The Hamptons is the seaside on eastern Long Island’s South Fork, a popular summer resort area for wealthy New Yorkers.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Flowers and trains appear in this work, to which Nam June Paik added “AMTRACK” implying Amtrak, the US national railway service, along with the names of regions that the train connects; New York, Chicago and Santa Fe. Paik also specifies that the train is delivering 100 flowers. A fence-like form, running parallel with the puffing train and flowers, look like design patterns. The vehicles, one of the frequently used motifs in Paik’s drawings, recall the fact that the artist often drew an analogy between communication and transportation.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Nam June Paik’s drawings that look like children’s spontaneous doodling do not have a set format or a distinct theme, yet one can notice a recurrent composition. Tangled lines of primary colors in disarray suggest TV scanning lines; elements of nature such as flowers, the human face and body, and vehicles of transportation can be seen; and a certain composition to embrace all this. In this drawing, one can see star-like flowers fenced in, with cars filing past it.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Nam June Paik’s study drawings display a childlike and playful mood, and his typical drawings are composed of wild lines of different colors with certain subject matters drawn on top of the lines, as seen in this work. One of the often-drawn themes is a sun-like flower; tassels or musical notes dangling from the flowers’ leaves can also be seen. The layered strokes of lines appear primitive and primordial. The word “Eden” written on the upper-left corner seems to point to a bitter-sweet life.

artworks.medium: black & white photograph on baryta paper
artworks.description: Nam June Paik stood in front of a running projector during the New Cinema Festival I held at the Film-Makers’ Cinematheque in New York, and Peter Moore photographed the scene. An installation of the same title consists of an endless loop of an unexposed film running through a projector. The resulting projected image shows a surface illuminated by bright light, occasionally altered by scratches and dust particles on the surface of the damaged film material. When the viewer stands in front of the projector, the person’s contour and movement become part of the performance.

artworks.title: Museum Title
artworks.description: Provincial officials from Gyeonggi-do began a discussion with Nam June Paik from 2001, and upon signing an MOU in 2002, the project to build a museum for Paik went underway. Museum Title is a symbolic signboard made by Paik himself for the museum, in which he wrote two words “Nam June Paik” and “Museum” in Korean, English, and Chinese in red, blue, and green. Although Paik did not see the completion of the would-be Nam June Paik Art Center in his lifetime, the artist christened it “a house where the spirit of Nam June Paik lives on” as a way of suggesting the museum’s mission.

artworks.description: Nam June Paik inserted “V”s and spirals into the article “Florida Declares Bush’s Victory” in The Korea Times, dated November 28th, 2000. The neck-and-neck race of the presidential election of George W. Bush and Al Gore, which depended on the result of votes in Florida, was being called off. As the voting system using a punch card caused a problem with counting, the votes were counted manually. The first article reviews how former presidents try to leave their political legacy by building architecture, as the design of Bill Clinton’s Presidential Library was unveiled to the public. artworks.description: On the articles of the “Art Reviews” section in the Weekend edition of The New York Times dated December 15th, 2000, Nam June Paik marked lines of brown and purple. The first article introduces emerging artist-run spaces for hiking travelers in the rapidly gentrified Brooklyn neighborhoods of Williamsburg, Greenpoint, and Dumbo. The second article by the food critic Mimi Sheraton is titled, “My Bronx: Yesterday’s Heroes, upon Pedestals,” which talks about The Hall of Fame Art Gallery, a sculpture gallery located in the Bronx Community College.

artworks.description: Nam June Paik often used newspaper as canvas, highlighting an article or a photograph that interested him with multiple lines, certain words, or figures. In a way, Paik made newspaper clippings by adding his drawings. This specific one is The New York Times dated December 3rd, 2000, and on page 4 of the Weekly Review, Paik made lines and circles with red, blue, and purple.

Chronicle of a Beautiful Paintress, instructs Knowles to dye different national flags with her menstrual blood each month, the American flag in January, Burmese in February, Chinese in March, Ethiopian in April, French in May, German in June, Hungarian in July, Irish in August, Jamaican in September, Congolese in October,…

Birds that resemble a boomerang fly over the mountains; the “v” sign was frequently used by Paik to symbolize the TV…

artworks.description: Nam June Paik wrote the Chinese phrase, “一色一筆,” which refers to ‘writing in one stroke of a brush in one color.’ A single red line runs above the phrase. This drawing recalls Paik’s action of drawing a line with his body, in such performances as Zen for Head (1961) and Zen for Walking (1961). The tip of the red line is slightly rolled up in a spiral form, which is typical of Paik’s representation of a wound-up videotape or a watch. Paik often made a comparison between a videotape that could be rewound and time in our life that is irreversible.

A similar form of the sun can be seen in Nam June Paik’s video installation Earth, Moon and Sun (1990). The work also looks like a dazzling flower with purple leaves and stem.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Strokes of countless lines in various colors seem to suggest action paintings. This is also reminiscent of a phrase in Paik’s lecture entitled Random Access Information, held in 1980. “I am confident that color video sets were invented by a genius, an artist. Television does not show image, only lines, like weaving. The difference between weaving and television is that television constantly weaves and that televised images can always be rewoven and woven again according to new motifs.”

artworks.description: After he collapsed by a stroke on April 20th, 1996, Nam June Paik had to rely on a wheelchair. Although the wheelchair with a bowler hat on it in the photograph seems to have a solitary atmosphere, Paik’s artistic passion never died. In a video recording of his performance at Anthology Film Archives in New York the year after, we can see him on a wheelchair breaking and knocking down the piano despite his impaired mouth and arms. artworks.description: Four flowers are portrayed like lollipops on the upper half of this work. On the lower half, a multiplex house with a tiled roof can be seen, with cars and bicycles passing by on the road in front of the house. The far-right side of the drawing reads “WINTER” in vertical; green buds sprout at the bottom, and flowers look like the glowing sun. This work seems to portray an urban cityscape around the time when the cold winter is moving out.  .

artworks.description: This work features various animals: a giraffe, a dog, a turtle, a monkey, a crab, fish, a duck and an octopus. “NJP” is written under the tiger-like animal, implying that the animal is Nam June Paik himself. The elongated tiger’s tail is rolled up in spirals here and there, which recalls Paik’s mentioning a Korean proverb that says, “Seeing a tiger’s tail is more frightening than seeing the tiger itself.” Animals such as fish, tigers, and turtles are motifs often used in Paik’s video installations.

A closer look at the drawing reveals that the pollen-like dots inside the pink circle on the right is repeated in the animal-like figure on the left, in a similar position.

Opposing traditional theater that required performers to strictly follow the script, Higgins, who sought ‘abstract’ plays, saw that actions and sound made by the human body could be formed like calligraphy patterns from the environment and materials of the stage: the Graphis series was its record. artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: This work is full of disheveled lines as if made by the hand that is moving free of will. In trying to follow the movement of the lines in yellow, green, red, and blue, one may identify untidy alphabets or notes and clefs on musical scores. While other drawings of Nam June Paik at least provide a hint on the subject matter, this work is closer to an abstract sketch.

artworks.description: Blast Theory is a collective artist group formed by Matt Adams, Ju Row Farr, and Nick Tandavanitj in London in 1991. The group has continuously pulled down the boundary between the public and the private through various media, creating a new space for public art. The group won the Nam June Paik Art Center Prize in 2016. The Thing I’ll Be Doing For The Rest Of My Life was created in line with a video of the same title. artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Nam June Paik often incorporated mixed alphabets and letters of Chinese, Korean, and English into his works. This calligraphic work contains strong cursive writing. Notable words are “love,” “every day,” and especially the first word, “Amor Fati,” in Chinese characters. Part of Nietzsche’s philosophy, the word refers to the love of fate, which is more than just accepting it but affirming and embracing it as one’s own, and cultivating it to grow into creativity. Interestingly, Paik added “AI,” which is Japanese pronunciation of ‘love’, in English next to 愛, to love.

artworks.title: David Bowie
artworks.description: 대중문화의 요소들은 Nam June Paik의 작품이나 텍스트에 자주 등장한다. 그의 위성 오페라 3부작에서는 미술계에서 활동하는 예술가들과 팝 가수 같은 대중문화 예술가들이 위계나 구분 없이 한데 어우러졌다. 그 중 한 명인 데이비드 보위는 Nam June Paik의 1988년작 〈세계와 손잡고〉에 출연해 〈성난 얼굴로 돌아보라〉를 부르며 현대무용그룹 라라라 휴먼 스텝스와 함께 공연했다. Nam June Paik은 여기에 라이브 비디오 합성 영상을 결합하여 방송되도록 하였다. 1994년부터 보위를 주제로 한 몇 가지 캔버스 작품을 만들었는데, 이 painting 작품은 영상 속 보위의 스틸 이미지에 픽셀 색상표 같을 것을 결합시킴으로써 디지털 이미지처럼 보이도록 했다.

artworks.description: This is a poster of the 1950 comedy film Blonde Dynamite starring the Bowery Boys and Leo Gorcey. The Bowery Boys was a fictional gang of New York City, and the characters were the subject of feature films released by Monogram Pictures from 1946 through 1958. On the poster, Nam June Paik painted a human body similar to the upper half of a seated Buddha statue, whose long arms were stretched out to embrace all the filmic characters. Paik put the year and his signature on the chest and wrist of the actress Adele Jergens.

artworks.title: NEO-DADA in der Musik, Kammerspiele, Dusseldorf
artworks.description: Among the occasions where Paik’s early performances were premiered was Neo-Dada in der Musik in the Kammerspiele Theater, Dusseldorf in 1962. Co-directed by Paik and George Maciunas, this Fluxus event featured Carlheinz Caspari, Benjamin Patterson, Tomas Schmit, and Wolf Vostell, with Jean-Pierre Wilhelm’s opening remarks. The fifth segment of the event featured a simultaneous performance of various artists’works in a parallel presentation. The photograph shows parallel performances of artists including Paik’s, in Neo-Dada in der Musik .

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Untitled is reminiscent of Nam June Paik’s personified televisions, as four short lines represent the eyes, nose, and mouth. The artist, however, omits the rectangular outline of the television. Three dots forming a vertical line can be seen below one of the eyes and the mouth, respectively, which may convey a certain emotional expression. The background is heavily painted in black, and the layers display various colors as if the brush was dipped with those colors all at once.

artworks.title: Untitled
artworks.description: Untitled is a drawing for Good Morning Mr. Orwell (1984). “Rendez-vous céleste” is written on the top, and two sets of three televisions are drawn at the bottom, with “Paris” written on the left and “N.Y.” on the right. Boomerang forms that Paik often employed to symbolize a TV antenna are flying upward and converge into “Rendez-vous céleste.” In an essay that Nam June Paik wrote on Good Morning Mr. Orwell, he explains that the satellite art project, which brings geniuses and stars of Earth that has never met or worked before, is “a high-tech version of the legend of Altair and Vega.”

artworks.description: The atelier of Mary Bauermeister in Cologne was a stronghold of artistic experimentation and often a venue for premieres of Fluxus performances. It was here in June 1960 that Contre-Festival zum Kölner IGNM-Fest was organized against the conservatism of International Society for New Music (IGNM, Internationale Gesellschaft für Neue Musik). Some artists from IGNM, and others who were ruled out by jury members of IGNM gathered in the atelier for readings, happenings, and musical concerts. The figure holding a ladder in the picture is Karlheinz Stockhausen.

artworks.description: Whenever artistic ideas came to mind, Nam June Paik whimsically scribbled them out, unhesitatingly on whatever was available at the moment, on the margins of book pages or on a restaurant’s napkins. artworks.title: Danger Music for Dick Higgins
artworks.description: Dick Higgins was an artist who framed the art of Fluxus, which saw art as a media of form that mixes various artistic genres with the concept of the intermedia. His Danger Music series of the early 1960s is based on the idea that scores could endanger their performers or the audience who experience the performance. Paik composed a score that wrote, “creep into the vagina of a living whale,” in response to Higgins’s scores. Nam June Paik wrote this score in English on a paper scroll and signed it in the bottom right corner.

artworks.title: Bathroom with Mannequin in Bathtub, Exposition of Music — Electronic Television, Galerie Parnass, Wuppertal
artworks.medium: black & white photograph on baryta paper
artworks.description: A mannequin lies in a bathtub with its head dipped under the blood-red water, both arms and one leg dismembered, and the other leg raised over the tub. In this space that looks like a horrifying mutilation murder scene, Nam June Paik made performance by looking down at the tub wearing a black garment and a white mask. According to the texts in the score, Moving Theater, these space installations and performances are related to political situations. In his first exhibition, Paik surprised many by installing what seemed like a combination of political awareness and the language of horror movies.
